title: Kirby's Dream Land
principle: Lower risks deliberately when targeting newcomers
why: He wanted the first Kirby to be as accessible as possible for new players; inhaling enemies and flying both reduced the risks players faced, and he kept going despite staff asking 'Are you sure about this?'
how: Give players tools that cut risk (fly over pits, neutralize enemies) while keeping some penalty, such as losing a life if you do fall.
anti_pattern: Making games unreasonably hard, which leaves beginners out in the cold.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale-and-spit and flight.
quote: Inhaling enemies and flying both reduced the potential risks players faced during gameplay.

title: Kirby's Dream Land
principle: Don't punish minor mistakes like missed jumps with instant death
why: Being hit and missing a jump are not serious mistakes, yet even games with health bars made falling an instant death; he thought losing a life for a missed jump was too harsh.
how: Keep a penalty for falling but give players a way to recover, such as the ability to fly over gaps.
anti_pattern: Treating every small slip as the harshest failure.
example: Kirby's Dream Land flight.
quote: I gave him the ability to fly because I thought it was too harsh to lose a life just for missing a jump.

title: Risk and Reward
principle: Tune player hitbox size as a core balance parameter
why: In Space Invaders the cannon's width determines how great your risk is; a different size could change how deep and engaging the game is. Mechanics that vary risk, like hiding halfway under a bunker, also matter.
how: Treat character size, hitboxes and partial cover as levers that set how risky approaching is, and tune them deliberately.
anti_pattern: Treating character size as purely visual design.
example: Space Invaders cannon width and bunkers.
quote: Your cannon's width is key to game balance because it determines how great your risk is.

title: Risk and Reward
principle: Don't add powerful options that erase risk without counterweights
why: A three-way laser in Space Invaders might look cool but probably wouldn't be good design, unless enemies also shot diagonally or ammo were limited.
how: Before adding a strong option, check what risk it removes and counterbalance it, for example with limited ammo.
anti_pattern: Cool-looking power-ups that remove the push and pull.
example: Hypothetical three-way laser in Space Invaders.
quote: Imagine how Space Invaders would feel with a three-way laser. It might look cool, but it probably wouldn't be the best game design.

title: Risk and Reward
principle: Dial game essence down for a broad audience
why: His theory is that as you increase game essence, you reduce a game's broad appeal; he made the first Kirby deliberately simpler to reach a wider audience.
how: Decide how much push and pull your target audience wants and simplify for wide audiences.
anti_pattern: Assuming more depth is always better for everyone.
example: Kirby's Dream Land, made deliberately simpler.
quote: As you increase "game essence," you reduce a game's broad appeal.

title: Kirby's Adventure
principle: Layer optional depth over a simple core both audiences can use
why: In a matured NES market with few beginners, he needed to satisfy both beginners and veterans; copy abilities let novices finish with inhale-and-spit while experienced players dig deeper.
how: Build a minimal core that can finish the game, add an optional depth system on top, and verify a core-only playthrough works.
anti_pattern: Requiring the depth system to progress.
example: Kirby's Adventure copy ability.
quote: Players who aren't used to complex game mechanics can finish the game just by inhaling enemies and spitting them out.

title: Kirby's Adventure
principle: Rebalance an overpowered ability through context before cutting it
why: More screen space made flight able to bypass nearly any challenge; he considered removing it but instead expanded the info panel, kept mid-boss fights to one screen and reduced flight speed, ending up nicely balanced.
how: Constrain a too-strong mechanic by shrinking play space, confining key fights to one screen, or lowering its speed.
anti_pattern: Cutting a signature mechanic outright.
example: Kirby's Adventure flight and its expanded info panel.
quote: I actually thought about removing flight entirely, but decided against it in the end.

title: Game Essence in Role-Playing Games
principle: Offset easy exits with harder individual battles
why: Games that let you exit dungeons at will or skip resource stress are more casual, but raising the difficulty of individual battles keeps a nice balance.
how: If you remove exploration risk, add challenge back into each fight.
anti_pattern: Removing all tension along with the exploration risk.
quote: By increasing the difficulty of individual battles, they can still hit a nice balance.

title: Kirby Super Star
principle: Raise enemy durability when moves gain variety and strength
why: Copy abilities gained many moves via repeat presses, directional inputs and commands; enemies that survive a few hits let stronger moves set abilities apart.
how: When adding moves of differing power, make standard enemies take several hits so strength differences show.
anti_pattern: One-hit enemies that make every move equal.
example: Kirby Super Star copy abilities vs. Kirby's Adventure's one move per ability.
quote: To compensate, we gave even standard enemies the ability to survive a few hits.

title: Keeping Rewards in Sight
principle: Make key purchases scarce, costly and powerful
why: In Faxanadu, a few expensive items that give a massive boost make players scrounge for money and plan toward the next gear; generous money and lots of equipment make this fun harder to provide.
how: Limit shop items to a few high-impact pieces priced so saving for them is a goal.
anti_pattern: Flooding players with money and minor gear.
example: Faxanadu shops.
quote: The player scrounges for money, thinking about how much more they need for the next big piece of gear— a real plus for the game.

title: The Fiend's Cauldron
principle: Let players wager currency on difficulty for proportionally bigger rewards.
why: A big risk for a big reward creates game essence and rewards strong play, which ordinary difficulty settings don't.
how: Charge currency to raise intensity, boost enemy aggression, attack and defense, and pay out more currency and better items on a clear.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron.
quote: If you take a big risk, you can get a big reward.

title: The Fiend's Cauldron
principle: Lower difficulty automatically after failure instead of offering Easy Mode.
why: Players rarely get stuck, it stings less than bluntly asking them to switch to Easy, and nobody has to play the whole game on Easy.
how: When an attempt fails, reduce the difficulty for the retry and take part of the player's stake as the cost.
anti_pattern: Bluntly prompting failing players to switch to Easy Mode.
example: Hearts spilling from the Fiend's Cauldron on failure.
quote: The system automatically lowers the difficulty when you fail, so the player rarely gets stuck.

title: The Fiend's Cauldron
principle: Clearly teach beginners how to lower the difficulty.
why: Players weren't told clearly enough that going below Intensity 2.0 lowered difficulty, and newcomers needed that most.
how: Introduce the lower-difficulty option explicitly to new players, not just the high-risk end.
anti_pattern: Leaving the easy side of a difficulty system unexplained.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Intensity below 2.0.
quote: Newcomers to the game are the ones who needed this most.

title: The Fiend's Cauldron
principle: Balance risk-and-reward systems against approachability.
why: Game essence makes games gamelike but can make them less approachable, especially on a small screen; constant pressure feels too hardcore.
how: Check stage length, enemy density and respawn points so the risk system doesn't make the whole game feel hardcore.
anti_pattern: Stages too big, with too many enemies, and no respawn where you died.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's land stages.
quote: Game essence, push and pull, and risk and reward are great for making the experience "gamelike," but they can conversely make games feel less approachable, too.

title: Modern Quality of Life Features
principle: Lock difficulty-lowering assists behind an explicit unlock step
why: The extra step prevents accidental changes, and such assists are acceptable because there's more to the game than fighting your way to the end.
how: Group assists like invisibility, slow motion, grab protection, infinite breath and puzzle skips under a locked menu, and offer presets that set many options at once.
anti_pattern: Difficulty-lowering options that can be switched on by accident.
example: The Last of Us Part I Combat Accessibility and Invisibility Toggle
quote: Requiring this extra "unlock" step is a great way to prevent players from accidentally changing certain options.

title: Meteos
principle: Lock processing speed before final balance tuning
why: He tuned every planet himself, but processing speeds changed late in development and the game ended up harder than intended.
how: Freeze frame timing and processing speed before final tuning, and redo balance passes after any late performance change.
anti_pattern: Changing processing speed after balance has been tuned.
example: Meteos released more difficult than he intended.
quote: I personally tuned the balance for each individual planet, but we changed processing speeds late in dev, resulting in a game that was more difficult than I intended.

title: Do Competitive Games Have to Be Complex?
principle: Size a game's depth to how many matches it must sustain
why: Casual fun has its place, but a game meant to last hundreds of matches needs a certain level of complexity, and moves too hard to perform hide the push and pull.
how: Decide the target lifespan first, then add depth to match while keeping inputs easy enough to feel the push and pull.
anti_pattern: Inputs so hard players can't feel the push and pull.
example: The original Street Fighter (1987) had many moves that were too hard to pull off.
quote: Still, if you want your game to last through hundreds upon hundreds of matches, its mechanics will need to deliver a certain level of complexity.

title: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking
principle: Smooth growth-stage power dips so players don't hit a wall
why: In pet games, growth stages are stronger or weaker than others, which can stall players in battle.
how: Check each growth stage's battle strength and adjust opponents or stats so no stage becomes a wall.
quote: In pet games, different growth stages will be stronger or weaker than others. So, we took care not to let players run into a wall in battles.

title: Development Secrets of the Original Kirby
principle: Make bosses big so newcomers' near-miss attacks still connect
why: Kirby was made for newcomers, so even slightly off-target attacks should still hit; ROM limits led to Whispy Woods being one mirrored piece placed three times on the background.
how: In beginner-focused games, give bosses large bodies, building them from background art if the sprite budget is tight.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: Whispy Woods.
quote: Kirby was a game made for newcomers, so even attacks that are slightly off-target should still hit.

title: Mountain Climbing Is More Than Just Climbing
principle: Don't scale enemy strength in direct proportion to player growth
why: A steady incline the whole way is a chore, especially with unchanging scenery or only periodic rest stops: it's just work.
how: Plot player vs. enemy strength and reshape it into peaks of challenge and flat stretches.
anti_pattern: A straight diagonal line of player and enemy strength rising together.
example: Mountain-climbing analogy.
quote: My point is, it's not a good idea to keep player and enemy strength in direct proportion.

title: Mountain Climbing Is More Than Just Climbing
principle: Avoid level-scaling enemies alongside the player
why: If enemies get stronger along with the player, you remove any incentive for getting ahead.
how: In open, multi-direction games, find balancing that keeps growth rewarding and leaves room for interesting strategies.
anti_pattern: Enemies that always scale to the player's level.
quote: If you include a system where enemies get stronger along with the player, you'll remove any incentive for getting ahead.

title: Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Slow the pace and input density for casual audiences
why: Melee's speed was great for top players but too harsh on new players, even causing tendinitis; the Wii targeted casual players, sideways Wii Remotes, and laggy online where dense inputs make frame skips stand out.
how: Lower game speed and the input density required, and tune toward casual play when the platform or audience calls for it.
anti_pattern: Keeping a hardcore, high-speed control scheme for a casual audience.
example: Super Smash Bros. Melee → Brawl.
quote: So, we kept the game's speed a little slower. And we tuned it more toward casual gameplay.

title: Make Retries Quick
principle: Keep a real cost to failure; avoid mindless in-place respawns
why: Infinite chances to respawn right where you died can make the game feel mindless, so speed must be balanced against penalty.
how: Pick a middle ground on checkpoint distance and penalties that suits your game's intent.
anti_pattern: Unlimited respawns at the exact spot of death.

title: Make Retries Quick
principle: Don't let enemies hit players the moment they respawn
why: If players keep losing without even touching the controller, they won't want to try anymore.
how: Place respawn points where no enemy can attack the player right away.
anti_pattern: Respawning players into enemy fire.

title: Is Your Game Appealing Enough to Start Over?
principle: Plan what stuck players will see on repeated attempts
why: If more players than expected hit a wall, they may keep seeing the same things again and again and quit.
how: For each likely failure point, list what players replay on the way back, then shorten it or vary it.
anti_pattern: Low-variety content that players must repeat many times.

title: Is Your Game Appealing Enough to Start Over?
principle: Don't judge difficulty by your own ability to scrape by
why: What keeps players going depends on volume, story and how fleshed out the game is, not on other games being hard or on the developer clearing it.
how: Test difficulty with players outside the team and assume more of them will hit walls than you expect.
anti_pattern: Assuming players will persist because hard games are popular.
quote: just because other games are hard, or because you can scrape by in the game you created, don't assume players will want to stick with it.

title: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U
principle: Use variable character strength for party modes, not level-playing-field matches
why: A framework that changes character parameters enabled Smash Run, Smash Tour, custom moves, Mii Fighters and trainable amiibo, but it isn't suited to hardcore matches that need a level playing field.
how: Build a parameter layer (equipment, attack/speed boosts, three variants per special move) and enable it only in casual or party modes.
anti_pattern: Letting stat-altering systems leak into serious competitive play.
example: amiibo CPU fighters that earn battle experience as they fight. Character Creation with three options for each special move.

title: Unexpected Results
principle: Fix post-launch difficulty problems with contained tweaks, not core rewrites
why: Adjusting the core CPU functions or each mode's difficulty would have meant bug-testing many game elements again, so narrower fixes were the only practical option.
how: Lower the difficulty of specific encounters or add an easier difficulty option through a patch, leaving core systems untouched.
anti_pattern: Rewriting core AI or global difficulty late, forcing wide re-testing.
example: Smash Ultimate: Challenger fights made easier and a Very Easy difficulty added to World of Light.

title: More Game Essence Means Less Broad Appeal
principle: Choose your target audience first, then set risk to match
why: Who you target should depend on your game's design and concept. A minor risk to an experienced player can be a brick wall to a beginner.
how: Write down the target player, then tune risk dials (threat range, hit count, escape tools, control inertia) to their skill.
anti_pattern: Tuning risk to your own skill level and assuming everyone perceives difficulty the same way.
example: Kirby's Dream Land was built for beginners and accomplishes exactly what it set out to do.
quote: Start by understanding how game essence arises, and use that knowledge to hone in on a target audience.

title: More Game Essence Means Less Broad Appeal
principle: Give beginners tools that neutralize threats before risk gets high
why: In Kirby's Dream Land, inhale stops enemies while the risk is still low, six hits of health and on-demand flight soften penalties, and that's what makes it approachable.
how: For a beginner audience, add generous neutralizing range, a forgiving health pool and an escape option from the steepest penalties.
anti_pattern: Harsh penalties like one-hit deaths or heavy inertia in a game meant for newcomers.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale, a spit attack with more range than the inhale, six hits of health, flight to avoid pits.
quote: We should be kind to beginners.

title: Special Crossover! #1
principle: Use asymmetric fail conditions so mismatched players enjoy the same game
why: Sakurai gave himself a one-hit loss while the guest played to game over, and framed it as shared fun rather than a contest with a winner and a loser.
how: In co-play between players of very different skill, give the stronger player a stricter fail condition and move on together when either fails.
anti_pattern: Framing every mismatched session as a strict head-to-head competition.
example: The Space Invaders Decade challenge with Arino Kacho.
quote: But I don't think we have to frame this as a competition with one winner and one loser.

title: Special Crossover! #2
principle: Let players push difficulty back through an enemy table they influence
why: Xevious has no AI reading your skill; its predefined enemy tables advance as you play, and destroying the radar-station enemy sends you back earlier in the table, making the game easier.
how: Drive spawns from an ordered table that advances with progress or skill, and add one recognizable target that rewinds it when destroyed.
example: Xevious — the radar-station-like enemy rewinds the enemy table
quote: Defeating one brings you back earlier in the enemy table, making the game easier.

title: Special Crossover! #2
principle: Don't strip every power-up on death in a power-up-driven game
why: In games with extreme power-ups like Gradius, losing everything after one death is no fun and makes players want to quit.
how: When a death costs the player their build, check whether they can still realistically recover from that point; if not, soften the loss.
anti_pattern: Resetting all power-ups so a late-game death leaves the player hopelessly underpowered.
example: Gradius — reaching a late area with only a Double cannon after losing power-ups
quote: It's no fun when you lose a life and all your power-ups reset.

title: Special Crossover! #3
principle: Offer a no-penalty trial period so newcomers can learn first
why: Space Harrier's 'trial time' let players die as much as they wanted for a while; many arcades kept it on for customers, and Sakurai turned it on to give Arino a fair start.
how: Add an opening window or optional mode where deaths cost nothing, then switch to normal rules.
example: Space Harrier — 'trial time'
quote: It means that during that time, you can die as much as you want.

title: Special Crossover! #3
principle: Use difficulty and resource settings as handicaps between unequal players
why: With no lives setting in The Genji and the Heike Clans, Sakurai took the hardest difficulty and fewest candles and gave Arino the easiest difficulty and most candles, making the contest fair.
how: Expose difficulty and resources (lives, health, enemy aggression) as separate per-player settings so a stronger player can handicap themselves.
example: The Genji and the Heike Clans — hardest/fewest candles vs. easiest/most candles
quote: There was no way to set the number of lives, so I put myself at the hardest difficulty with the lowest number of candles.

title: Special Crossover! #3
principle: Check that co-op doesn't make the game harder than solo
why: In two-player Darius the ships get in each other's way and power-ups only cover one ship, which actually makes it harder; Contra's two-player scroll point sits far forward, which makes it tough.
how: Playtest co-op for shared power-ups budgeted for one player, players blocking each other, and a camera or scroll point that strands the trailing player.
anti_pattern: Dropping a second player into single-player resource and camera tuning unchanged.
example: Darius two-player power-ups; arcade Contra two-player scroll point
quote: The two ships get in each other's way, and you only get enough power-ups for one ship— which actually makes it harder.

title: The Shoryuken Command
principle: Reward full command inputs, but never make them mandatory in casual games
why: Ryu's full-command shoryuken in Smash is stronger with more invincibility, but making it essential would have split players who can and can't execute it, so it stayed casual-friendly.
how: Offer a one-button version of special moves and give the full command a modest bonus such as extra damage or invincibility frames.
anti_pattern: Balancing so a hard input is required to compete.
example: Super Smash Bros. — Ryu's one-button vs. command shoryuken
quote: For the sake of keeping things casual, we went ahead with the current balance.

title: The Pros and Cons of Leaderboards
principle: Hide the top player and wall off the elite in their own tier
why: Seeing how far you are from the world's best makes people give up, and the info only matters to the very elite; Elite Smash gives top players status and keeps them from matching lower-ranked players.
how: Don't surface the #1 player's identity or score to general players; create an elite tier that matches top players with each other.
anti_pattern: Showing everyone their distance from the top.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — GSP obscures the top player; Elite Smash
quote: Players will just see how far away they are and want to give up.

title: The Pros and Cons of Leaderboards
principle: Balance matchmaking range between finding matches and fair skill gaps
why: Players need opponents of similar skill who are also nearby and online at the same time, which is rare in low-population areas; too narrow means no match, too broad means mismatches.
how: Tune the skill range by region and time of day, widening it only as far as needed for players to find matches.
anti_pattern: A fixed range that is either too narrow or too broad.
quote: If the matching range is too narrow, players will never find a match, but if it's too broad, players will match with people far outside their skill level.

title: Randomness Spices Games Up
principle: Never let luck alone decide a player's loss
why: Losing only because of bad luck is hard to accept; players need to feel responsible for their own failure.
how: Give players ways to respond to random events or control them, and keep randomness out of strict skill contests.
anti_pattern: Relying on a luck stat players forget or won't invest in.
example: Peach's Smash Attack, once random, is now chosen with up or down; Wizardry's 1981 luck stat.
quote: In a game, players need to feel to some extent like they're responsible for their own failure.

title: Randomness Spices Games Up
principle: Keep randomness that still demands skill or enables comebacks
why: Random elements are acceptable when using them well takes skill, and random items give anyone a chance to come back in a fun-first game.
how: Allow randomness like a random command list that each needs skill, and random items in casual modes.
example: Smash Bros.: the Hero's randomized command list and markedly random items.

title: Handicap Systems
principle: Give casual competitive games catch-up mechanics so wins rotate
why: Games where the most skilled player wins every time aren't fun, and in an average household different people should take turns winning.
how: Give trailing players speed boosts or stronger items, as Mario Kart does, and accept that the leader can be dethroned.
anti_pattern: Letting the most skilled player win every match in a casual game.
example: Mario Kart's speed boosts and items for trailing players.
quote: Games where the person with the most skill keeps winning every single time just aren't fun.

title: Handicap Systems
principle: In skill-driven games, level the field through chaos, not stat buffs
why: Sakurai wanted Smash results to reflect skill, so trailing players get no attack or knockback help, while chaotic items, stages and Final Smashes still shake up outcomes.
how: Make power-ups harder for the leader to obtain and charge comeback meters faster for losing players, leaving core stats untouched.
anti_pattern: Raising attack power or reducing knockback for players who are behind.
example: Smash Bros.: the leader has a harder time getting a Smash Ball, and the Final Smash Meter charges faster for losing players.
quote: In other words, chaotic, anything-goes content like Final Smashes, items, stages, and even Final Smash Meters are a great fit for a party game, I’d say.

title: Handicap Systems
principle: Design local multiplayer to tolerate quirks players can house-rule
why: At home, players can talk out their differences, and banning a cheap move becomes part of the fun or a memory, so a bit of weirdness is OK.
how: When designing mainly for local play, accept minor exploits players can ban themselves, and offer an optional automatic handicap setting.
example: Sakurai's Smash Bros. Brawl proposal noted the game targets home play and is in some ways unsuited to online play.
quote: So it's OK if there's a bit of weirdness there.

title: Better Than Not Being Able to Beat the Game
principle: Let players change difficulty at any time without restarting
why: Games that force a restart because difficulty can't be adjusted have a fundamental design flaw, since once players give up, the challenge is worthless.
how: Make the difficulty setting available mid-playthrough and keep all progress when it changes.
anti_pattern: Locking difficulty at the start so a stuck player has to start over.
quote: Simply letting them change difficulties whenever they want should make a big difference.

title: Better Than Not Being Able to Beat the Game
principle: Offer stuck players an easier mode or a skip after repeated failures
why: In action games you can't win just by getting stronger, and everyone has a breaking point, so a slightly humiliating offer beats being unable to finish.
how: After several failures in one spot, offer to lower the difficulty or skip the stage as if cleared, worded so it doesn't humiliate the player.
anti_pattern: An impossible difficulty spike at the end of a long game.
example: Some games recommend lowering the difficulty after repeated failure; others let you skip difficult stages.
quote: Even if you diminish the very gameplay itself, that's still better than not being able to beat it.

title: Better Than Not Being Able to Beat the Game
principle: Choose hardcore difficulty deliberately, knowing not every player wants it
why: Some pleasures only come from intense, unforgiving battles, and hardcore games can be smash hits, but it's best to assume not all players will go for that.
how: If you go hardcore, make it an explicit design goal; otherwise default to kindness, as Kirby's Dream Land did for beginners.
example: Kirby's Dream Land was tailored to beginners from its inception.
quote: However, it's best to assume that not all players will go for that in every game.

title: Average and Mediocre Are the Same Thing
principle: Offset strong traits by amplifying weaknesses, not by cutting strengths
why: Balancing purely on strength patches shortcomings and trims advantages until fighters are average, and average isn't fun.
how: When a character overperforms, first exaggerate its weaknesses, and reject proposals that sand away its signature strengths.
anti_pattern: Trimming advantages and patching weaknesses until everyone is average.
example: Smash Bros. tuning team proposals steered to keep fighters unique.
quote: Hence, I advise our team to keep fighters unique by amplifying shortcomings to offset advantages.

title: Average and Mediocre Are the Same Thing
principle: Validate balance with real win-rate data, but trust how characters feel
why: Smash Bros. Ultimate's global online data put all 87 fighters between 47.18% and 51.43%, showing unique fighters can still be balanced, but feel is the true metric.
how: Collect win rates from real matches to confirm every character has a shot, then make final calls based on how each character feels.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's online win rates: highest 51.43%, lowest 47.18%.
quote: I'm not saying that win rates are everything, as the true metric is how each fighter feels

title: Play Testing Keeps Going
principle: Judge balance beyond top-tournament usage, including multiplayer matches
why: A wide spread of fighters at top tournaments is good, but some fighters are naturally better tuned for multiplayer matches.
how: Check how characters perform in multiplayer matches as well as in tournament usage before deciding they need changes.
anti_pattern: Judging fairness from one part of the game in isolation.
quote: I'm glad that top tournament players use a wide range of fighters, but that's not the only thing we look at.

title: Computer-Controlled Players
principle: Give CPU players human-like reaction delays
why: CPUs that react faster than a human can feel extremely unfair, and players already tend to suspect computers of cheating.
how: Add a reflex delay before CPUs respond, and let status effects like reversed controls briefly confuse them before they adapt.
anti_pattern: Superhuman reaction speed.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate CPUs have a 'reflex' and get somewhat confused by reversed controls.
quote: if they react faster than a human can, it can feel extremely unfair to players.

title: Computer-Controlled Players
principle: Tune top-level CPUs for aggressive offense, not perfect defense
why: Players who choose high CPU levels want strong opponents, and waiting, machine-like reflexes or perfect shields would make CPUs invincible but no fun.
how: Bias high-difficulty AI toward attacking and winning, accept weaker defense and evasion, and cap perfect shields and dodges.
anti_pattern: CPUs that always perfect-shield or dodge every attack.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate CPUs were tuned more aggressively than in past titles.
quote: In the end, it's important to remember that our goal is to make things as fun as possible.

title: Game Essence in Strategy Games
principle: Build counter cycles with clear weaknesses and fitting resource costs
why: Clear strengths, weaknesses and appropriate costs enrich the game, and differences in power or abilities add depth.
how: Create cycles like infantry, tanks, helicopters, anti-air, and vary units by cost, attack power and abilities such as leaping over others.
anti_pattern: Adding complexity without allocating strengths and weaknesses wisely.
example: Infantry lose to tanks, tanks to helicopters, helicopters to anti-air cannons, anti-air to infantry.

title: Game Essence in Strategy Games
principle: Question whether random evasion is needed in strategy combat
why: A game will likely work without random dodge chances; they keep players on their toes but can feel unfair.
how: Prototype without randomness first, and add it only if the uncertainty is worth the unfairness it brings.
anti_pattern: Random rolls that swing the same battle unpredictably.

title: How Good Were the Player’s Actions?
principle: Scale rewards and penalties to how good the action really was
why: Players are happiest when their behavior is compensated correctly, and success and failure should each have a fitting consequence.
how: For each reward, penalty and damage value, ask how good or bad the triggering action was; give more points for stronger, harder enemies.
anti_pattern: Pushing the mapping so far that the game becomes predictable.
example: Score games award more points by enemy strength and difficulty, and can add location-based damage or breakable parts.

title: How Good Were the Player’s Actions?
principle: Decide how players can recover from bad irreversible choices
why: A big penalty for a really bad action can be fun, but you must ask whether the player can ever redeem themselves and how much effort it takes.
how: Review irreversible choices by how bad the action was, not just scenario logic, and set an explicit path and cost to recover.
anti_pattern: Permanent penalties decided only by scenario logic.

title: Being Kind to Beginners
principle: Lower the barrier to entry until new players are fully drawn in
why: There's no point in playing if you're not having fun, and it's hard enough to get people to play at all, so beginners who get crushed may abandon the game.
how: Audit the path from first boot until a player is hooked, in single-player and competitive modes, and remove barriers along it.
anti_pattern: Letting newcomers be flattened before they understand the game.
example: The King of Fighters '95: Sakurai crushed a couple who had just come to try the game, and has mostly avoided playing strangers since.
quote: Ultimately, there's no point in playing games if you're not having fun. As such, it's important to be kind when introducing new players to a title.

title: Amplify Both Strengths and Weaknesses
principle: Keep each option's peaks and valleys instead of averaging them out
why: The more alike fighters' abilities become, the more they feel like the same character, which gives the whole game a bland feel; variety is what keeps it fresh.
how: When something is too strong, don't also soften its weaknesses; keep a distinct strength and weakness for every option, in competitive and non-competitive games alike.
anti_pattern: Shaving down a strength while lessening the weaknesses to compensate.
example: Smash Bros. fighter balancing, driven by the Balancing Team's daily matches and online match data.
quote: Variety among things like fighters is the very lifeblood of the game!

title: Amplify Both Strengths and Weaknesses
principle: Nerf a secondary parameter and leave the move's defining strength intact
why: One attack has many components (power, speed, duration, windup, follow-through, range, hit size, animation speed, knockback, combo ability, shield damage, shield recovery), so it can be weakened without erasing its character.
how: Keep the characteristic attack power but lengthen the vulnerable follow-through, or shrink the hitbox.
anti_pattern: Flattening the stat that makes the move distinctive.
example: Smash Bros. move adjustments.
quote: leave the move's characteristic attack power untouched, and instead lengthen the follow-through— a time when the fighter is vulnerable.

title: Give Yourself a Handicap When Balancing Your Game
principle: Don't use the dev team's skill as the difficulty standard
why: Team members know the game inside out, so tuning to the best player, or even the median one, leaves it too hard for players who won't spend all their time on your game.
how: Set difficulty a good deal below what feels right to the team, then make it easier still.
anti_pattern: Balancing around the most skilled player on staff.
quote: developers who already know a game shouldn't be considered as the standard— instead, make the game even easier than you think it should be, and it'll be just right.

title: Give Yourself a Handicap When Balancing Your Game
principle: Handicap yourself while tuning difficulty
why: Playing one-handed makes even someone who knows the game well slip up, which brings the developer closer to a typical player.
how: Test with one hand on the controller, reduced health, or stricter conditions, and tune so you can still clear it.
example: Sakurai plays with one hand when balancing.
quote: Playing the game with one hand, for example. It's easy to mess up even if I know the game well, so this is certainly an effective method.
